name: Professional extractions / acne facial
lead: Professional comedone extraction is the manual removal of blackheads and whiteheads by an esthetician or dermatologist, usually as part of an acne facial. People use it to clear clogged pores that make skin look rough, dotted or congested, and to get a smoother, clearer surface without the damage that can come from squeezing at home.[1]

A comedo is a hair follicle plugged with keratin and oil. It is open (a blackhead, dark because of oxidation rather than dirt) or closed (a whitehead).[1] Dermatologists can often remove open comedones with little trauma to the skin, while closed ones are harder to extract.[1] Salons and clinics use comedo extractors and typically steam the face or wash it with warm water first, with attention to hygiene.[1] Wikipedia's Comedo article describes extraction as safest in trained hands.[1]

In dermatology guidance, extraction sits alongside medical acne care rather than in place of it. A 2026 clinical update in Australian Prescriber describes light-based and physical therapies, comedone extraction among them, as useful adjuncts that are ideally accessed through dermatologists, with topical retinoid and benzoyl peroxide combinations as first-line treatment for most patients.[6]

No published trial has tested esthetician extractions themselves; the practice is described mainly in dermatology references and encyclopedic summaries, alongside research on related acne and pore-care products.[1][2][6]

chain: Steaming or warm washing softens the plug
Extractor clears the blackhead or whitehead
Smoother, less congested skin with less picking damage
angle.text: Extraction physically removes the keratin and oil plugs that show up as blackheads and whiteheads, so the skin looks clearer and more even soon afterwards. People also use it as a controlled alternative to squeezing, which is associated with scarring and marks.

infobox: Described as an adjunct to medical acne therapy[6]

paras: Comedo extractors are used in salons and by dermatologists, normally after steaming the face or washing with warm water.[1] Open comedones tend to come out with minimal skin trauma, whereas closed comedones are harder to remove.[1]

Larger comedones of about 1 mm or more (macrocomedones) may be removed with surgical instruments or cauterised with a light-based device. Because isotretinoin can cause severe flare-ups of these lesions, dermatologists often remove them before and during that treatment.[1]
Dermatologists can also use cyanoacrylate to lift blackheads across an area, a stronger method than over-the-counter pore strips, which are gentler but can still damage skin.[1]

Comedones are the visible hallmark of acne: Wikipedia's acne article states that blackheads and whiteheads must be present for a diagnosis of acne, and describes the first change as an invisible microcomedone that grows as dead skin cells and sebum accumulate.[4] Blackheads darken when the plug is exposed to air.[4] Clearing them is therefore one of the most direct ways to change how the skin surface looks and feels.

Acne is very common. Wikipedia reports that it affected about 633 million people worldwide in 2015 and that an estimated 80-90 percent of teenagers in Western countries have it, with close to half of those affected still having it in their twenties and thirties.[4] The same article notes that acne can lower confidence and self-esteem, which is one reason skin clarity features so heavily in appearance discussions.[4]

Extraction is one of several ways comedones are managed. Others include topical retinoids and azelaic acid, which Wikipedia notes appear beneficial without increasing pigmentation, and laser treatment, which may reduce comedones although lasers and dermabrasion have been known to cause scarring.[1]

Dermatology literature on post-acne marks notes that lesions that have been traumatised are a recognised risk factor for acne-induced hyperpigmentation, particularly in people with darker skin tones, which is one reason skin-care discussions emphasise gentle handling of lesions.[3]

Scars result from inflammation in the dermis; Wikipedia's acne article estimates that scarring affects 95 percent of people with acne vulgaris, with atrophic scars the most common type at roughly 75 percent of cases, and notes that post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation is more common in darker skin and can often be prevented by avoiding aggravating lesions.[4] A 2026 review of acne-induced hyperpigmentation likewise lists traumatised lesions as a recognised risk factor.[3]

For some people, picking becomes a repetitive behaviour in its own right. Excoriation (skin-picking) disorder was listed as a separate condition in the DSM-5 in May 2013; its Wikipedia article reports prevalence estimates of about 1.4 to 5.4 percent, notes that for some people it begins with adolescent acne and continues after the acne clears, and says habit reversal training and cognitive behavioural therapy are among the approaches used.[5] Practitioners of professional extraction often frame the facial as an alternative to self-squeezing; no study has compared the two.

In appearance communities, professional extractions are discussed as a periodic facial for blackheads and congestion and as a substitute for self-squeezing. Discussion centres on skin clarity and on avoiding the marks and scars that picking can leave. Extraction is typically mentioned as one step in a wider skin routine that includes cleansers, retinoids and sunscreen; the Comedo article notes that retinoids are best applied at night with sunscreen in the daytime.[1] Community accounts describe the practice in general terms and the wiki does not rely on any single thread.

Squeezing or picking can damage the skin, raise the risk of infection and scarring, and may push infection deeper.[1] Pore strips may leave pores open and remove surface skin, and dermabrasion and laser can cause scarring.[1] Excessive washing or scrubbing can irritate skin and worsen comedones.[1]

No studies found. Related clinical research has examined topical products for oily skin, blackheads and enlarged pores; one 56-day trial evaluated an emulsion containing niacinamide and plant extracts for acne and conspicuous pores, but it did not test manual extraction.[2] Reviews of acne management mention extraction as an adjunct without reporting trial data of its own.[6]

timeline.event: English dermatologist Erasmus Wilson introduces the term 'neurotic excoriation' for compulsive skin picking.[5]
Louis-Anne-Jean Brocq publishes the first known print description of an adolescent who picked at her acne.[5]
The US iPLEDGE programme for isotretinoin begins, the drug for which dermatologists often clear macrocomedones first.[4][1]
The DSM-5 lists excoriation (skin-picking) disorder as its own condition.[5]
A 56-day trial of a niacinamide emulsion for acne and conspicuous pores is published.[2]
Australian Prescriber's acne update lists comedone extraction among adjunct physical therapies.[6]

lore.intro: Extractions come up in skin-care discussion as the professional alternative to squeezing at home, and as one component of a clear-skin routine.[1]

claims.claim: Professional extraction is gentler on skin than squeezing at home.
claims.believers: Users say trained hands, steaming and clean tools reduce scarring and infection compared with picking.
claims.experts: Dermatology references say squeezing carries infection and scarring risk and describe professional extraction as done with careful hygiene; no controlled comparison has been published.[1]

claims.claim: A facial can clear blackheads without further treatment.
claims.believers: Practitioners and clients describe visibly cleaner skin right after a session.
claims.experts: References describe extraction as removing existing comedones, while retinoids and azelaic acid are described as treatments that act on comedone formation.[1]

claims.claim: Squeezing at home causes scars and marks that a professional visit avoids.
claims.believers: Users say that leaving extraction to trained hands, with steaming and clean tools, protects against the dark marks and pits they associate with picking.
claims.experts: Dermatology references list squeezing as a risk for infection and scarring, and review literature names traumatised lesions as a risk factor for post-acne hyperpigmentation.[1][3] No trial has compared professional and home extraction.

claims.claim: Extraction is a supplement to a routine, not a replacement for it.
claims.believers: Practitioners describe the facial as a periodic reset that works alongside retinoids and cleansers.
claims.experts: A 2026 clinical update describes extraction as a useful adjunct to first-line topical therapy, ideally through dermatologists.[6]

claims.claim: Picking can become compulsive and the facial can interrupt it.
claims.believers: Some people say regular professional care reduces the urge to squeeze.
claims.experts: Excoriation disorder is a recognised DSM-5 condition whose treatment literature centres on behavioural therapy and habit reversal; no study has examined facials for this purpose.[5]

card.summary: Manual blackhead and whitehead removal by a pro; standard practice, with little formal trial evidence.
card.note: Poorly done extraction can cause infection or scarring.

quick.overview:
Professional extraction is manual removal of blackheads and whiteheads by an esthetician or dermatologist, often during an acne facial.

Open comedones are generally easier to remove than closed ones. Sources found no controlled trials specific to the practice.
quick.mechanism: A comedo extractor applies pressure to expel the keratin and oil plug, usually after steaming or warm washing.
quick.risks: Picking or squeezing risks infection and scarring; hygiene and technique matter, and dermabrasion or laser can also scar.
